issues: Verdict KNOWN upheld. The proof step is textbook LP and is correct: positive coordinates on S have inactive bounds, so rank |F| forces the coverage rows to have rank K on S, and the KxK system is invertible. The paper claims no novelty for it. The bertsimas1997 [Thm 2.3] citation is confirmed through sources I fetched and read myself: the arXiv 2302.12364 text ('basic feasible solutions are precisely extreme points (vertices) ... (Bertsimas and Tsitsiklis, 1997, Theorem 2.3)'), Wikipedia (Def. on p. 50, ISBN 978-1-886529-19-9, which matches ISBN-10 1886529191) and the MIT OCW 6.251J lecture 2 slide (vertex <=> extreme point <=> BFS; BFS = tight rows span R^n). I could not fetch the book itself (athenasc.com SSL failure). The theorem and page numbers therefore rest on secondary sources, though they are consistent. The Chebyshev analogy is loose. The closer classical analogue is the Shapley-Snow (1950) kernel theorem for matrix games: a square nonsingular submatrix fixes an extreme optimal strategy. Crossref confirms that paper exists (DOI 10.1515/9781400881727-004, AM-24 pp. 27-36), but I could not fetch its content (HTTP 405/429). It is an optional, unverified pointer and not a recommended citation. Process issue relevant to the slowness: in this session the WebSearch budget is used up (200/200), and the arXiv and Semantic Scholar APIs return HTTP 429. Later verifiers cannot search at all.
